events.title: Early Human Settlement
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows early human activity in present-day Nigeria. Stone tools discovered on the Jos Plateau prove late Paleolithic human habitation. These early inhabitants were hunter-gatherers who gradually developed agriculture and animal husbandry.

events.title: Neolithic Cultural Development
events.description: The Nigerian region saw more complex cultural developments during the Neolithic period, including refined pottery making and stone tool craftsmanship. Archaeological discoveries show that inhabitants of this period had mastered agricultural techniques, beginning to cultivate tubers and grains. Social organization became more complex, with specialized division of labor emerging.

events.title: Bronze Age Begins
events.description: The Nigerian region entered the Bronze Age, with local craftsmen mastering bronze smelting technology. Bronze was mainly used for religious rituals and as symbols of social status, reflecting social stratification. This period also witnessed the development of long-distance trade.

events.title: Rise of Nok Civilization
events.description: The Nok civilization was one of the earliest known civilizations in West Africa, famous for its exquisite terracotta sculptures. Located in central Nigeria, the Nok people mastered iron-working technology, making them one of the first peoples south of the Sahara to use iron. Their artworks demonstrated highly developed culture and religious beliefs.

events.title: Early Urbanization
events.description: Various regions in Nigeria began experiencing early urbanization, with some settlements developing into regional political and commercial centers. These early cities had defensive fortifications, markets, and craft districts, showing further development of social organization.

events.title: Iron Age Begins
events.description: The Nigerian region entered the Iron Age, with mastery of iron technology promoting agricultural development and population growth. Iron tools increased agricultural productivity, making more complex social organizations possible. This period also witnessed the expansion of trade networks.

events.title: Decline of Nok Civilization
events.description: The Nok civilization began to decline, possibly due to factors such as climate change, population pressure, or foreign invasions. Despite the civilization's decline, Nok artistic traditions and technical knowledge had profound influences on later cultures.

events.title: Regional Trade Networks Expand
events.description: Extensive trade networks formed between different regions of Nigeria, exchanging iron tools, pottery, food, and other goods. These trade connections promoted cultural exchange between different regions and accelerated technology transfer. Trade routes along the Niger and Benue Rivers were particularly important.

events.title: Early Political Organization Development
events.description: Various regions in Nigeria began forming more complex political organizations, with chieftaincy systems and hereditary rule emerging. These early political entities controlled trade routes, organized public works, and established legal systems. The centralization of political power created conditions for the rise of later kingdoms.

events.title: Rise of Trans-Saharan Trade
events.description: Northern Nigeria began participating in trans-Saharan trade, establishing commercial links with North Africa. Main trade goods included gold, ivory, slaves, and salt. The development of trade promoted the rise of cities and the spread of Islam.

events.title: Kanem-Bornu Empire Established
events.description: The Kanem-Bornu Empire was established around Lake Chad, controlling vast territories including present-day northeastern Nigeria. This empire became an important trade center, controlling trans-Saharan trade routes, especially in slaves, ivory, and salt. The empire adopted Islam, becoming a major force in the Islamization of the region.

events.title: Institutionalization of Hausa City-States
events.description: Hausa city-states developed mature political institutions, including electoral systems, legal frameworks, and military organizations. The city-states had both competition and cooperation among them, forming complex political networks. This system laid the foundation for later political development.

events.title: Rise of Hausa City-States
events.description: The Hausa people established multiple city-states in northern Nigeria, including Kano, Katsina, and Zaria. These city-states were famous for trade and crafts, particularly textiles and leather goods. Hausa city-states became important nodes in trans-Saharan trade, promoting the spread of Islam.

events.title: Islam Consolidates in the North
events.description: Islam further consolidated in northern Nigerian regions, becoming the primary religion of the ruling class. Islamic scholars established schools and libraries, promoting Arabic literacy and Islamic law. This period witnessed the fusion of Islamic culture with local traditions.

events.title: Ife Kingdom Established
events.description: The Yoruba people established the Ife Kingdom in southwestern Nigeria, considered the birthplace of Yoruba civilization. Ife was famous for its exquisite bronze and terracotta artworks, demonstrating highly developed artistic skills. The Ife Kingdom held a sacred position in Yoruba religion and culture.

events.title: Benin Empire Established
events.description: The Edo people established the Benin Empire in southern Nigeria, with its capital at Benin City. The empire was famous worldwide for its exquisite bronze artworks and ivory carvings. The Benin Empire developed complex political systems and military organizations, controlling important trade routes.

events.title: Golden Age of Yoruba Civilization
events.description: Yoruba civilization entered its golden age, with cities like Ife and Oyo becoming important political and cultural centers. Artistic achievements of this period reached their peak, particularly in bronze sculpture and ivory carving. The Yoruba also developed complex religious and philosophical systems.

events.title: Oyo Empire Established
events.description: The Yoruba people established the Oyo Empire, becoming one of the most powerful empires in West Africa. The Oyo Empire was famous for its powerful cavalry forces, controlling vast territories extending from southwestern Nigeria to Benin and Togo. The empire established complex political systems, including mechanisms to check royal power.

events.title: Benin Empire Expansion
events.description: The Benin Empire reached its zenith, controlling vast territories from Lagos to the Niger Delta. The empire established powerful military forces and efficient administrative systems. Benin bronze craftsmanship reached unprecedented levels.

events.title: Portuguese Arrival
events.description: Portuguese explorer Rui de Sequeira reached the Nigerian coast, becoming the first Europeans to reach the region. The Portuguese initially engaged mainly in trade activities, exchanging European goods for ivory, pepper, and later slaves. This marked the beginning of European contact with Nigeria.

events.title: Oyo Empire at Its Peak
events.description: The Oyo Empire became one of the most powerful political entities in West Africa, with its cavalry forces dominating the region. The empire established complex tribute systems and trade networks, controlling important trade routes. Oyo's political system influenced the entire Yoruba region.

events.title: Introduction of European Firearms
events.description: European merchants introduced firearms to Nigeria, changing the local military balance. Kingdoms with firearms gained military advantages, which intensified regional conflicts and promoted the development of the slave trade. The introduction of firearms marked a major transformation in military technology.

events.title: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
events.description: Nigeria became one of the major sources of the trans-Atlantic slave trade, with millions of Nigerians forcibly transported to the Americas. This trade had devastating effects on local societies, causing population decline, social upheaval, and political instability. Some coastal kingdoms, such as Calabar and Bonny, actively participated in the slave trade.

events.title: Institutionalization of Slave Trade
events.description: The trans-Atlantic slave trade became fully institutionalized in coastal Nigeria, forming complex networks of capture, transport, and sale. Some kingdoms specialized in the slave trade, establishing corresponding political and economic institutions. This system caused profound trauma to society.

events.title: Spread of New Crops
events.description: New crops from the Americas such as maize, cassava, sweet potatoes, and peanuts became widely cultivated in Nigeria. These high-yield crops improved food security, supported population recovery and growth, and also changed traditional agricultural structures.

events.title: Usman dan Fodio's Jihad
events.description: Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio launched a jihad, overthrowing the rulers of Hausa city-states and establishing the Sokoto Caliphate. The goal of this jihad was to purify Islamic practices and establish a true Islamic state. The Sokoto Caliphate became one of the largest political entities in 19th century West Africa.

events.title: British Abolition of Slave Trade
events.description: After Britain abolished the slave trade, it began patrolling the West African coast to prevent slave trading. Britain established a foothold in Lagos and began promoting legitimate trade, particularly palm oil trade. This marked the beginning of British influence in Nigeria.

events.title: Return of Freed Slaves
events.description: Thousands of freed slaves returned to Nigeria from Sierra Leone, Brazil, and the West Indies, particularly to the Lagos area. These returnees brought new technologies, commercial knowledge, and cultural influences, becoming catalysts for early modernization. They established new communities and introduced European architectural styles and lifestyles.

events.title: Christian Missionary Activities
events.description: European Christian missionaries began large-scale missionary work in southern Nigeria. Missionaries established schools, hospitals, and churches, introducing Western-style education and medical services. The spread of Christianity formed complex interactions with traditional religions and later Islam.

events.title: Peak of Exploration Activities
events.description: European explorers such as Heinrich Barth and Richard Lander conducted deep explorations into Nigeria's interior, mapping territories and studying local cultures and resources. These exploration activities provided important geographical and cultural information for later colonial rule.

events.title: British Bombardment of Lagos
events.description: The British Navy bombarded Lagos, forcing local rulers to sign anti-slave trade treaties. This military action was an important step in Britain's expansion of influence in the region, laying the foundation for later colonial rule.

events.title: Lagos Becomes British Colony
events.description: Britain formally annexed Lagos, making it a British colony. This was the beginning of British direct rule in Nigeria. Lagos became Britain's administrative and commercial center in the region.

events.title: Intensified Colonial Competition
events.description: Colonial competition among Britain, France, and Germany in the Nigerian region intensified. Countries expanded their influence by signing treaties, establishing trading posts, and sending military expeditions. This competition ultimately led to the convening of the Berlin Conference in 1884.

events.title: Royal Niger Company Established
events.description: Britain established the Royal Niger Company, obtaining a charter to conduct trade and administrative management in the Niger River basin. The company controlled trade in the region and gradually expanded British political influence.

events.title: Modern Infrastructure Development
events.description: The British colonial government began building modern infrastructure in Nigeria, including railways, telegraph lines, and port facilities. These infrastructures primarily served the colonial economy but also promoted modernization. Infrastructure construction required large amounts of labor, changing local labor relations.

events.title: Benin Expedition
events.description: Britain launched the Benin Expedition, capturing Benin City and ending the independence of the Benin Empire. British forces looted numerous Benin bronzes and ivory carvings, which remain in British museums today. This expedition marked the strengthening of British control over southern Nigeria.

events.title: Northern Nigeria Protectorate Established
events.description: Britain established the Northern Nigeria Protectorate, with Frederick Lugard as High Commissioner. Britain began implementing indirect rule in the northern region, governing through local chiefs and emirs. This system preserved traditional political structures but placed them under British supervision.

events.title: Conquest of Sokoto Caliphate
events.description: British forces captured Sokoto, ending the independence of the Sokoto Caliphate. The last Caliph Attiku was deposed, and Britain established complete colonial rule in northern Nigeria. This marked the incorporation of all major Nigerian political entities into the British colonial system.

events.title: Lagos Railway Opens
events.description: The railway line from Lagos to the interior opened, Nigeria's first railway. Railway construction greatly promoted economic development, particularly exports of cocoa, peanuts, and palm oil. However, the railway primarily served the colonial economy, transporting raw materials to the coast for export.

events.title: Coal Mining Begins
events.description: Britain began commercial coal mining in Enugu, marking the beginning of Nigeria's modern mining industry. Coal mines provided energy for railways and industry but also brought labor exploitation and environmental destruction. Coal miners became the core of Nigeria's early working class.

events.title: Tin Mining Development
events.description: Tin mining on the Jos Plateau developed rapidly, attracting numerous British mining companies. Tin became an important export commodity, but mining activities destroyed local agriculture and environment. The influx of migrant workers also changed local demographic structure and social relations.

events.title: Amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria
events.description: Britain merged the Northern Nigeria Protectorate and Southern Nigeria Protectorate to form the Colony of Nigeria. Lugard became the first Governor-General, establishing a unified colonial administrative system. This amalgamation created the borders of modern Nigeria but also forcibly combined different ethnic groups and cultures.

events.title: World War I Impact
events.description: Thousands of Nigerian soldiers were conscripted to fight in World War I, serving in East Africa and other battlefields. War experiences broadened their horizons, and many veterans returned home to become supporters of nationalist movements. The war also caused economic difficulties and rising prices.

events.title: Influenza Pandemic
events.description: The Spanish flu caused a severe epidemic in Nigeria, with an estimated 500,000 deaths. The epidemic exposed the inadequacy of the colonial medical system and triggered discontent with colonial rule. This pandemic also promoted public health awareness.

events.title: Emergence of Nationalism
events.description: Western-educated Nigerian intellectuals began forming nationalist consciousness, demanding more political rights and self-governance. This period saw the emergence of the first political organizations and newspapers, laying the ideological foundation for later independence movements.

events.title: First Higher Education Institution
events.description: Higher education institutions such as Yoruba College (predecessor of University of Lagos) began to be established. Western education cultivated a new intellectual class who became leaders of anti-colonial movements and nationalism. Educational expansion also exacerbated development gaps between north and south.

events.title: Aba Women's War
events.description: Igbo women in the Aba region launched large-scale protests against British colonial government tax policies and indirect rule system. This protest, called the 'Aba Women's War,' was one of the most important resistance movements during Nigeria's colonial period. British military suppression resulted in dozens of women's deaths.

events.title: Cash Crop Economy Development
events.description: The cultivation of cash crops such as cocoa, peanuts, and palm oil developed on a large scale in Nigeria. These crops became important export commodities, bringing foreign exchange revenue to the colony. The development of the cash crop economy changed agricultural structures and social relations.

events.title: First Strike Movement
events.description: Large-scale strikes erupted in Lagos and other cities, with workers demanding improved working conditions and higher wages. The strikes marked the rise of organized labor movements, with unions becoming important forces in anti-colonial struggles. Colonial government was forced to implement some labor reforms.

events.title: World War II Impact
events.description: About 100,000 Nigerian soldiers fought for Britain in World War II, participating in campaigns in Burma and elsewhere. War experiences greatly enhanced national consciousness, and postwar veterans actively participated in independence movements. The war also brought economic opportunities and promoted industrial development.

events.title: Political Awakening Movement
events.description: After World War II, Nigeria's political awakening movement reached its climax. Various political parties were established successively, labor movements emerged, and public demands for independence grew stronger. This period laid the political foundation for independence in 1960.

events.title: General Strike Movement
events.description: A nationwide general strike paralyzed major cities, with tens of thousands of workers participating. The strike demanded improved living conditions and political rights, showing strong public discontent with colonial rule. This strike became an important catalyst for postwar independence movements.

events.title: Richards Constitution
events.description: Britain promulgated the Richards Constitution, establishing Nigeria's federal structure by dividing the country into Northern, Western, and Eastern regions. This constitution first gave Nigerians representation in the central government, though power remained limited.

events.title: University College Established
events.description: University College Ibadan (later University of Ibadan) was established, Nigeria's first university. The university's establishment marked important development in higher education, training a generation of indigenous intellectuals and political leaders. The university also became an important dissemination ground for nationalist thought.

events.title: Federal System Establishment
events.description: Britain established a federal system in Nigeria, dividing the country into three regions: Northern, Western, and Eastern. The federal system aimed to balance the interests of different regions and ethnic groups but also sowed the seeds for later political divisions.

events.title: Macpherson Constitution
events.description: The new constitution expanded Nigerian political participation, establishing more representative legislative institutions. This constitution laid the foundation for Nigerian self-government and promoted the development of party politics.

events.title: Kano Riots
events.description: A visit by southern politicians to Kano triggered serious riots, reflecting deepening political divisions between north and south. The riots resulted in dozens of deaths, exposing the fragility of Nigerian national unity. This incident accelerated the establishment of federal system.

events.title: Lyttleton Constitution
events.description: This constitution established true federalism, giving regions greater autonomy. Nigeria was formally called the 'Federation of Nigeria,' preparing for independence. The regions gained internal self-government.

events.title: First Commercial Oil Extraction
events.description: Shell Oil Company conducted first commercial oil extraction in the Niger Delta. The discovery of oil would completely transform Nigeria's economic and political landscape. However, oil extraction also brought environmental destruction and social conflicts, particularly in oil-producing regions.

events.title: Western and Eastern Regions Independence
events.description: Nigeria's Western and Eastern regions gained internal self-government, with only foreign affairs and defense remaining under British control. This was an important step toward complete independence.

events.title: Niger River Bridge Completed
events.description: The Niger River Bridge connecting Onitsha was completed, one of the longest bridges in West Africa. The bridge greatly improved transportation between east and west, promoting economic integration. This project demonstrated progress in modern infrastructure construction.

events.title: Northern Region Independence
events.description: The Northern region also gained internal self-government, making all Nigerian regions internally self-governing. The same year saw the last pre-independence elections.

events.title: Independence of Nigeria
events.description: Nigeria gained independence, becoming a dominion within the Commonwealth. Abubakar Tafawa Balewa became the first prime minister. Independence celebrations were held in Lagos, marking the end of British colonial rule. Nigeria became the most populous independent country in Africa.

events.title: Republic Established
events.description: Nigeria became a republic, no longer recognizing the British monarch as head of state. Nnamdi Azikiwe became the first President. This marked Nigeria's complete break from British political control.

events.title: Western Region Crisis
events.description: A serious political crisis erupted in Nigeria's Western Region, with electoral fraud triggering large-scale violent conflicts. The crisis exposed the fragility of Nigeria's political system and created conditions for the military coup of 1966.

events.title: First Military Coup
events.description: Young officers staged a coup that overthrew the civilian government. Prime Minister Balewa and several political leaders were killed. The coup was led mainly by Igbo officers, which provoked resentment and fear in the northern region. General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi became head of state.

events.title: Counter-Coup
events.description: Northern officers staged a counter-coup, overthrowing and killing Aguiyi-Ironsi. Lieutenant Colonel Yakubu Gowon became head of state. The coup intensified ethnic tensions, especially the antagonism between the north and the east.

events.title: Anti-Igbo Massacres
events.description: Large-scale massacres of Igbo people occurred in the northern region, with tens of thousands killed and millions fleeing back to the eastern region. These violent events further intensified ethnic hatred, setting the stage for civil war.

events.title: Republic of Biafra Declares Independence
events.description: Odumegwu Ojukwu, the military governor of the Eastern Region, declared the Eastern Region's secession from Nigeria and the founding of the Republic of Biafra. The decision was a response to anti-Igbo violence and political marginalization. Biafra was recognized by a few countries, but most of the international community supported Nigerian unity.

events.title: Nigerian Civil War (Biafran War)
events.description: Civil war erupted between the Nigerian federal government and the Republic of Biafra. The war lasted 30 months, causing enormous humanitarian disaster. The Biafran region was blockaded, leading to severe famine with an estimated 1-3 million deaths, mostly civilians. The war attracted international attention and humanitarian aid.

events.title: Biafra Surrenders
events.description: The Biafran forces surrendered and the civil war ended. Ojukwu went into exile in Côte d'Ivoire. The Gowon government announced a policy of "no victor, no vanquished" in an attempt to achieve national reconciliation. Postwar reconstruction began, focusing on reintegrating the Eastern Region.

events.title: Oil Boom
events.description: Nigeria's oil industry developed rapidly, with oil revenues increasing dramatically. The 1973 oil crisis caused oil prices to soar, bringing Nigeria enormous income. The government launched large-scale infrastructure projects, but this also led to corruption and economic dependence on oil.

events.title: Nationalization of Oil
events.description: The Nigerian government began the process of nationalizing the oil industry and founded the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC). The nationalization policy aimed to increase state control of oil resources but also brought problems of managerial efficiency and corruption.

events.title: Gowon Overthrown
events.description: General Murtala Mohammed staged a bloodless coup that overthrew the Gowon government. The new government promised reforms, a fight against corruption, and a timetable for the transition to civilian rule. The Mohammed government was popular with the public.

events.title: Assassination of Mohammed
events.description: Murtala Mohammed was assassinated in an attempted coup. Lieutenant General Olusegun Obasanjo succeeded him as head of state. Obasanjo continued to advance the plan for the transition to civilian rule.

events.title: Administrative Reorganization
events.description: The military government increased Nigeria's states from 12 to 19, aiming to weaken the power of large states and promote national unity. This administrative reorganization was an important milestone in Nigeria's political development, creating more balanced regional representation.

events.title: Second Republic Begins
events.description: Nigeria returned to civilian rule with Shehu Shagari elected as President. The new constitution established an American-style presidential system and created 19 states. The Second Republic marked the restoration of Nigeria's democratic system.

events.title: Religious Revival Movement
events.description: Nigeria experienced revival movements in both Christianity and Islam, with religion's influence in political and social life intensifying. The religious revival brought positive social changes but also exacerbated religious and regional tensions.

events.title: Buhari Coup
events.description: General Muhammadu Buhari staged a coup that overthrew the Shagari government and ended the Second Republic. The military government claimed the coup was meant to save the country from corruption and economic collapse. The Buhari government implemented harsh economic and social policies.

events.title: Babangida Coup
events.description: General Ibrahim Babangida overthrew the Buhari government. Babangida promised more flexible economic policies and a gradual transition to democracy. His rule lasted eight years, and he was nicknamed "Maradona" for his political dexterity.

events.title: Structural Adjustment Program
events.description: Under pressure from the World Bank and IMF, Nigeria implemented a Structural Adjustment Program. The program included currency devaluation, trade liberalization, and privatization. While aimed at improving the economy, it also led to social hardship and increased inequality.

events.title: Capital Relocation
events.description: Nigeria officially relocated its capital from Lagos to Abuja. The construction of the new capital aimed to create a neutral political center and promote national unity. The capital relocation was an important step in Nigeria's modernization process.

events.title: June 12 Election
events.description: A presidential election widely regarded as the freest and fairest in Nigerian history was held. Moshood Abiola won clearly, but the Babangida government annulled the result, triggering nationwide protests and a political crisis.

events.title: Babangida Steps Down
events.description: Under domestic and international pressure, Babangida was forced to step down. He appointed Ernest Shonekan as interim president, but this "Interim National Government" lacked legitimacy and support.

events.title: Abacha Coup
events.description: General Sani Abacha staged a coup that overthrew the Shonekan government. Abacha established a military dictatorship, suppressed the opposition, and imprisoned many political activists, including Moshood Abiola.

events.title: Execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa
events.description: The renowned writer and environmental activist Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogoni activists were executed by the Abacha government. They had protested the environmental damage caused by oil companies in the Niger Delta. The event drew international condemnation, and Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth.

events.title: Sudden Death of Abacha
events.description: General Sani Abacha died suddenly; the official cause was a heart attack. General Abdulsalami Abubakar succeeded him and promised a democratic transition. Abacha's death opened the way for Nigeria's democratization.

events.title: Death of Abiola
events.description: Moshood Abiola died in prison, just a day before his expected release. The official cause was a heart attack, but many suspected he had been poisoned. Abiola's death ended the 1993 election crisis but also became a tragedy in Nigerian political history.

events.title: Fourth Republic Begins
events.description: Olusegun Obasanjo was elected President, Nigeria returned to democratic rule, beginning the Fourth Republic. Obasanjo was a former military leader but returned as a civilian president. This marked the beginning of Nigeria's longest democratic period.

events.title: Niger Delta Conflict
events.description: Armed conflict erupted in the Niger Delta region, with local communities protesting environmental destruction and economic marginalization from oil extraction. Armed groups like the Movement for the Emancipation of the Niger Delta (MEND) launched attacks, kidnapped oil workers, and sabotaged oil facilities. The conflict seriously affected oil production.

events.title: Sharia Law Controversy
events.description: Twelve northern Nigerian states implemented Islamic Sharia law, triggering nationwide controversy. The implementation of Sharia law intensified religious and regional tensions, becoming a sensitive issue in Nigerian politics.

events.title: Religious Violence Escalates
events.description: Several northern Nigerian states implemented Islamic law (Sharia), triggering religious tensions. Violence between Christians and Muslims increased, particularly in the Middle Belt region. Thousands died in religious violence.

events.title: Debt Relief
events.description: Nigeria received substantial debt relief from the Paris Club, reducing external debt from approximately $30 billion to about $5 billion. Debt relief freed up fiscal resources for infrastructure construction and social development.

events.title: Yar'Adua Elected President
events.description: Umaru Musa Yar'Adua was elected President, marking the first civilian-to-civilian power transfer in Nigerian history. Although there were allegations of electoral fraud, this transition was seen as an important step in democratic consolidation.

events.title: Boko Haram Uprising
events.description: Islamic extremist group Boko Haram launched an uprising in Maiduguri, engaging in fierce clashes with security forces. The group's founder Mohammed Yusuf was killed, but the organization didn't disappear, instead becoming more radical and violent.

events.title: Yar'Adua Dies, Jonathan Succeeds
events.description: President Yar'Adua died from illness, and Vice President Goodluck Jonathan succeeded as President. Jonathan, from the southern Ijaw ethnic group, broke the long-standing pattern of northern Muslim control of the presidency, causing political tensions.

events.title: Jonathan Elected President
events.description: Goodluck Jonathan won the presidential election, but the results triggered violent protests in northern regions. Hundreds died in post-election violence, mainly due to religious and ethnic tensions.

events.title: Fuel Subsidy Protests
events.description: Government removal of fuel subsidies led to sharp increases in oil prices, triggering nationwide protests. The 'Occupy Nigeria' movement organized massive demonstrations, forcing the government to partially restore subsidies. These protests demonstrated the power of civil society.

events.title: Chibok Schoolgirls Kidnapping
events.description: Boko Haram militants kidnapped 276 schoolgirls from a school in the town of Chibok. The incident drew global attention, and the "Bring Back Our Girls" campaign won international support. Most of the girls have still not been rescued, and the case has become a symbol of Boko Haram's atrocities.

events.title: GDP Rebasing
events.description: Nigeria rebased its GDP calculations, becoming Africa's largest economy. The rebasing reflected rapid development in services and telecommunications sectors, but also exposed imbalances in economic structure.

events.title: Buhari Elected President
events.description: Muhammadu Buhari defeated incumbent President Jonathan in the presidential election, becoming the first candidate in Nigerian history to defeat a sitting president through elections. Jonathan conceded defeat and peacefully transferred power, seen as an important milestone for Nigerian democracy.

events.title: Economic Recession
events.description: Due to falling oil prices and the impact of Boko Haram conflict, Nigeria's economy fell into recession. This was the first recession in 25 years, with unemployment soaring and inflation rising. The government implemented various economic stimulus measures to try to revive the economy.

events.title: Some Chibok Girls Released
events.description: Through negotiations, 82 Chibok schoolgirls were released. This was a rare successful negotiation between the government and Boko Haram, but over 100 girls remain missing. The return of the released girls attracted national attention.

events.title: Farmer-Herder Conflicts Intensify
events.description: Conflicts between Fulani herders and farmers escalated dramatically, particularly in the Middle Belt region. Climate change, land scarcity, and religious differences intensified these conflicts. Thousands died in farmer-herder conflicts, becoming one of Nigeria's major security threats.

events.title: Buhari Re-elected
events.description: Muhammadu Buhari won re-election in the presidential election, defeating main opponent Atiku Abubakar. The election process was relatively peaceful, but there were still some violent incidents and allegations of fraud. Buhari promised to continue fighting corruption and terrorism.

events.title: EndSARS Protest Movement
events.description: Young people launched the EndSARS protest movement, demanding the disbandment of the Special Anti-Robbery Squad (SARS), which was accused of abuse of power and human rights violations. The protests spread across the country and won international support. The government announced the disbandment of SARS, but protests continued to demand broader police reform.

events.title: Lekki Toll Gate Shooting
events.description: Security forces opened fire on peaceful protesters at the Lekki Toll Gate in Lagos, causing several deaths and injuries. The incident became known as the "Lagos massacre" and drew international condemnation. The government denied the army's involvement, but video evidence showed a violent crackdown.

events.title: Lekki Toll Gate Incident
events.description: Security forces opened fire on peaceful protesters at Lekki Toll Gate in Lagos, causing multiple deaths and injuries. This incident became an important turning point in Nigeria's democratic development, triggering international concern about human rights.

events.title: Twitter Ban
events.description: The government indefinitely suspended Twitter operations in Nigeria after Twitter deleted President Buhari's controversial tweet. This decision drew international criticism, seen as an attack on free speech. The ban lasted 7 months before being lifted.

events.title: Security Crisis Worsens
events.description: Nigeria faced multiple security challenges: continued Boko Haram threats in the northeast, kidnapping and banditry in the northwest, farmer-herder conflicts in the Middle Belt, and separatist violence in the southeast. Thousands of schools closed, with millions of children out of school.

events.title: Bola Tinubu Elected President
events.description: Bola Tinubu won the presidential election and was due to take office in May 2023. The election was fiercely contested, and the young candidate Peter Obi won considerable support, especially among young voters. Tinubu's victory marked the return of power from the north to the southwest.

events.title: Tinubu Sworn In as President
events.description: Bola Tinubu was sworn in as Nigeria's 16th president, promising to address the economic and security challenges facing the country. In his inaugural speech he declared that "the fuel subsidy is gone," causing an economic shock. Tinubu faced enormous expectations and challenges.

events.title: Fuel Subsidy Reform
events.description: The Tinubu government abolished the long-standing fuel subsidy, causing gasoline prices to rise sharply. Although the decision was considered economically necessary, it also provoked strong public opposition and a sharp rise in the cost of living.

events.title: Ongoing Challenges
events.description: Nigeria continues to face multiple challenges: economic difficulties, high inflation, security threats, inadequate infrastructure, and governance issues. Despite rich natural resources and a large population, Nigeria still struggles to realize its potential. Young people constitute the majority of the population, with growing desire for change. The nation's future depends on addressing these deep-rooted problems, achieving inclusive growth and good governance.
